title: Needle in a haystack
subtitle: Grover's algorithm: mark the answer with phase and amplify it with interference.

steps.title: Searching without an index
body: Picture a list of N items in no particular order, and a way to check whether an item is the right one. Classically, you test one by one: N/2 tries on average.
In 1996, Lov Grover showed that a quantum computer needs about √N queries. For a million items: fewer than a thousand, instead of half a million.

steps.question: With 2 qubits there are 4 items. We put them all in superposition (H, H) and the oracle marks item 11 with a CZ. What's the chance of measuring 11 now?
steps.explain: Still 25%. The oracle marked 11 by flipping the sign of its amplitude — notice the bar's different color — but phase alone doesn't change probability. Interference is missing.

steps.title: Inversion about the mean
body: The next step is the diffuser: it reflects each amplitude about the average of all of them. The marked one, now negative, sits far below the average — and gets thrown way up. The others shrink.

With 2 qubits, a single round takes the marked item to 100%. As a circuit, the diffuser is: H on all, “mark |00⟩”, H on all. Marking |00⟩ can be done with X on all, CZ, X on all — or, shorter, Z on all and a CZ.

steps.title: Build the diffuser
steps.goal: The oracle (columns 0–1) marked 11. Build the diffuser so that 11 comes out with 100% probability.
hints: Start with H on both qubits.
Then mark |00⟩: Z on both and a CZ (or X on both, CZ, X on both).
steps.success: You found the needle with one query! With 4 items, a classical computer would need more than two on average.

steps.question: We change the oracle to mark 01 (X on qubit 0, CZ, X on qubit 0). Same diffuser. What's the chance of measuring 01?
steps.explain: 100%. The diffuser knows nothing about the answer: it just amplifies whatever is marked. The whole “question” lives in the oracle.

steps.question: For 1 million items, roughly how many queries does Grover need?

options.why: That's the classical average, testing one by one.
That would be an exponential speedup (≈ log₂N). For unstructured search, it's proven that √N is the best possible.
Only with 4 items! In general, it takes several rounds of oracle + diffuser — and overshooting makes the result worse.

steps.title: Grover and passwords
steps.text: Grover's speedup is “only” quadratic: brute-forcing a 128-bit key would drop from 2¹²⁸ to about 2⁶⁴ steps. That's why the advice is to use larger symmetric keys, like AES-256. The real threat to today's cryptography is Shor's algorithm, against RSA and elliptic curves.

takeaways: The oracle marks the answer by flipping its phase; the diffuser turns phase into probability.
Grover needs ~√N queries: a quadratic speedup, which is optimal for unstructured search.
Too many rounds overshoot: the number of iterations has to be calculated.
